title: Chapter 19 — Why So Many Ambitious Men And So Little Lofty Ambition Are To Be Found In The United States
paragraphs: To Be Found In The United States

The first thing that strikes a traveler in the United States is the countless multitude of those who seek to throw off their original condition; and the second is the rarity of lofty ambition to be observed in the midst of this universally ambitious stir of society. No Americans are without a yearning desire to rise; but hardly any seem to entertain hopes of great magnitude, or to aim at very lofty goals. All are constantly seeking to acquire property, power, and reputation—few contemplate these things on a great scale. This is all the more surprising because nothing is visible in the manners or laws of America to limit desire, or to prevent it from spreading its impulses in every direction. It seems hard to attribute this singular state of things to the equality of social conditions, for at the very moment when that same equality was established in France, the flight of ambition became unbounded. Nevertheless, I think that the principal cause of this fact is to be found in the social condition and democratic manners of the Americans.

All revolutions enlarge the ambition of men: this is particularly true of those revolutions that overthrow an aristocracy. When the former barriers that kept the multitude back from fame and power are suddenly thrown down, a violent and universal rise takes place toward that eminence so long coveted and at last within reach. In this first burst of triumph nothing seems impossible to anyone. Not only are desires boundless, but the power of satisfying them seems almost boundless, too. In the midst of the general and sudden renewal of laws and customs, in this vast confusion of all men and all ordinances, the various members of the community rise and sink again with excessive rapidity; and power passes so quickly from hand to hand that no one need despair of catching it in turn. It must also be remembered that the people who destroy an aristocracy have lived under its laws. They have seen its splendor, and they have unconsciously absorbed the feelings and notions it entertained. Thus at the moment when an aristocracy is dissolved, its spirit still pervades the mass of the community, and its tendencies are retained long after it has been defeated. Ambition is therefore always extremely great as long as a democratic revolution lasts, and it will remain so for some time after the revolution is complete. The memory of the extraordinary events men have witnessed is not erased in a day. The passions a revolution has roused do not disappear at its close. A sense of instability remains in the midst of re-established order: a notion of easy success survives the strange vicissitudes that gave it birth. Desires remain extremely enlarged, while the means of satisfying them diminish day by day. The taste for large fortunes persists, though large fortunes are rare; and on every side we trace the ravages of excessive and hapless ambition kindled in hearts that it consumes in secret and in vain.

At last, however, the final traces of the struggle are erased; the remnants of aristocracy completely disappear; the great events attending its fall are forgotten; peace succeeds war, and the rule of order is restored in the new realm. Desires are again adapted to the means by which they can be fulfilled; the wants, opinions, and feelings of men come together again; the level of the community is permanently fixed, and democratic society is established. A democratic nation that has reached this permanent and regular state of things will present a very different spectacle from the one we have just described. We may readily conclude that if ambition grows great while the conditions of society are growing equal, it loses that quality once they have grown so. As wealth is subdivided and knowledge diffused, no one is entirely without education or property. The privileges and disqualifications of caste being abolished, and men having shattered the bonds that held them fixed, the notion of advancement suggests itself to every mind, the desire to rise swells in every heart, and all men want to rise above their station. Ambition is the universal feeling.

But if the equality of conditions gives some resources to all members of the community, it also prevents any of them from having resources of great extent, which necessarily confines their desires within somewhat narrow limits. Thus among democratic nations ambition is ardent and continual, but its aim is not habitually lofty; and life is generally spent in eagerly coveting small objects within reach. What chiefly diverts the men of democracies from lofty ambition is not the smallness of their fortunes, but the intensity of the efforts they make daily to improve them. They strain their faculties to the utmost to achieve paltry results, and this cannot fail quickly to limit their vision and to narrow their powers. They might be much poorer and still be greater. The small number of opulent citizens to be found in a democracy are no exception to this rule. A man who raises himself by degrees to wealth and power contracts, in the course of this prolonged labor, habits of prudence and restraint that he cannot afterward shake off. A man cannot enlarge his mind the way he enlarges his house. The same observation applies to the sons of such a man. They are born, it is true, in a lofty position, but their parents were humble; they have grown up amid feelings and notions they cannot easily afterward get rid of; and it may be assumed that they will inherit the propensities of their father as well as his wealth. It may happen, on the contrary, that the poorest descendant of a powerful aristocracy may display vast ambition, because the traditional opinions of his race and the general spirit of his order still buoy him up for some time above his fortune. Another thing that prevents the men of democratic periods from easily indulging in the pursuit of lofty goals is the length of time they foresee must pass before they can be ready to approach them. "It is a great advantage," says Pascal, "to be a man of quality, since it brings one man as far forward at eighteen or twenty as another would be at fifty—which is a clear gain of thirty years." Those thirty years are commonly wanting to the ambitious men of democracies. The principle of equality, which allows every man to arrive at everything, prevents all men from advancing rapidly.

In a democratic society, as elsewhere, there are only a certain number of great fortunes to be made; and since the paths leading to them are indiscriminately open to all, the progress of all must necessarily be slowed. Since the candidates appear to be nearly alike, and since it is difficult to make a selection without infringing the principle of equality, which is the supreme law of democratic societies, the first idea that suggests itself is to make them all advance at the same rate and submit to the same probation. Thus, in proportion as men become more alike, and the principle of equality is more peaceably and deeply infused into the institutions and manners of the country, the rules of advancement become more inflexible, advancement itself slower, and the difficulty of arriving quickly at a certain height far greater. From hatred of privilege and from the awkwardness of choosing, all men are at last forced, whatever their standard, to pass through the same ordeal. All are indiscriminately subjected to a multitude of petty preliminary exercises, in which their youth is wasted and their imagination quenched, so that they despair of ever fully attaining what is held out to them. By the time they are finally in a condition to perform any extraordinary acts, the taste for such things has left them.

In China, where the equality of conditions is exceedingly great and very ancient, no man passes from one public office to another without undergoing a probationary trial. This probation is repeated at every stage of his career; and the notion is now so rooted in the manners of the people that I remember reading a Chinese novel in which the hero, after countless setbacks, succeeds at last in touching the heart of his mistress by taking honors. A lofty ambition breathes with difficulty in such an atmosphere.

The remark I apply to politics extends to everything; equality everywhere produces the same effects. Where the laws of a country do not regulate and retard the advancement of men by positive enactment, competition achieves the same end. In a well-established democratic community, great and rapid elevation is therefore rare; it forms an exception to the common rule, and it is the singularity of such occurrences that makes men forget how rarely they happen. Men living in democracies eventually discover these things; they find out at last that the laws of their country open a boundless field of action before them, but that no one can hope to cross it quickly. Between them and the final object of their desires, they see a multitude of small intermediate obstacles, which must be slowly surmounted. This prospect wearies and discourages their ambition at once. They therefore give up hopes so doubtful and remote, and search nearer to themselves for less lofty and more easily obtained enjoyments. Their horizon is not bounded by the laws, but narrowed by themselves.

I have observed that lofty ambitions are more rare in ages of democracy than in times of aristocracy. I may add that when, in spite of these natural obstacles, they do come into being, their character is different. In aristocracies the career of ambition is often wide, but its boundaries are fixed. In democracies ambition commonly ranges in a narrower field, but once it gets beyond that, hardly any limits can be set to it. Since men are individually weak, since they live apart and in constant motion, since precedents carry little authority and laws are of short duration, resistance to novelty is languid, and the fabric of society never appears perfectly upright or firmly consolidated. So that once an ambitious man has power in his grasp, there is nothing he will not dare; and when it is gone from him, he meditates the overthrow of the State to regain it. This gives great political ambition a character of revolutionary violence that it seldom shows to an equal degree in aristocratic communities. The common aspect of democratic nations will present a great number of small and very rational objects of ambition, from among which a few ill-controlled desires of a larger growth will at intervals break out; but anything like ambition conceived and carried out on a vast scale is not to be met with there.

I have shown elsewhere by what secret influence the principle of equality makes the passion for physical gratifications and the exclusive love of the present predominate in the human heart. These different propensities mingle with the feeling of ambition, and tinge it, as it were, with their hues. I believe that ambitious men in democracies are less engrossed than any others with the interests and the judgment of posterity; the present moment alone engages and absorbs them. They are more apt to complete a number of undertakings quickly than to raise lasting monuments of their achievements, and they care much more for success than for fame. What they most ask of men is obedience; what they most covet is empire. Their manners have in almost all cases remained below the height of their station. The consequence is that they frequently carry very low tastes into their extraordinary fortunes, and that they seem to have acquired supreme power only to minister to their coarse or paltry pleasures.

I think that in our time it is very necessary to cleanse, regulate, and adapt the feeling of ambition, but that it would be extremely dangerous to try to impoverish and repress it too much. We should try to lay down certain outer limits, which it should never be allowed to overstep; but its range within those established limits should not be checked too much. I confess that I fear much less for democratic society from the boldness than from the mediocrity of desires. What seems to me most to be dreaded is that, in the midst of the small, incessant occupations of private life, ambition should lose its vigor and its greatness—that the passions of man should slacken, but at the same time be lowered, so that the march of society should every day become more tranquil and less aspiring. I think, then, that the leaders of modern society would be wrong to lull the community with a state of too uniform and too peaceful happiness, and that it is good to expose it from time to time to matters of difficulty and danger, in order to raise ambition and give it a field of action. Moralists are constantly complaining that the ruling vice of the present time is pride. This is true in one sense, for no one thinks he is not better than his neighbor, or consents to obey his superior. But it is extremely false in another, for the same man who cannot endure subordination or equality has so contemptible an opinion of himself that he thinks he is only born to indulge in vulgar pleasures. He willingly takes up with low desires, without daring to embark on lofty enterprises, of which he scarcely dreams. Thus, far from thinking that humility ought to be preached to our contemporaries, I would have efforts made to give them a larger idea of themselves and of their kind. Humility is unwholesome to them; what they most need is, in my opinion, pride. I would willingly exchange several of our small virtues for this one vice.
